name: Aaron Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the corrugated-board line and measure the first sheet after the flutes change. I have a two-year technical diploma and am one of the best at tuning this corrugator, though the other operators know their sections too. A square stack is satisfying; a jammed roller on a rushed shift is not.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and how do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Nia works part-time in a hotel laundry, and our grown children live separately. We rent, my lead pay is low for this job, we have three weeks of expenses saved and few similar plants nearby. I use AI now and then for shift notes, but measure real sheets before I sign an order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the corrugated-board crew that a bit of AI help with delivery notes is worth keeping. The board still has to fold on the scored line and come out square.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can tune the corrugator by sound and lead the shift, but our pay has been stuck below what this skill should bring. My partner Nia works part-time in a hotel laundry, our grown children have their own places, and we have about three weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the corrugator running and measure the first sheet after a flute change. I use AI now and then to tidy delay notes, but check the actual order; I would put a small amount from each fresh full wage into savings only if rent and food are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious even if the technology stalls. A quiet AI year still has a rent date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a sheet square?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flute and liner must meet at the marked edge. If it is off by a finger width, a whole stack can fold badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change about pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring our lead-operator wage scale to the union meeting. My diploma and responsibility should show up in the weekly number.

say: I would keep **first-sheet checks** after every flute change on the corrugator.
I would raise **lead-operator wages** at the next union bargaining meeting.
think: Our **three-week reserve** cannot cover a long missed shift.
Nia’s **part-time laundry wage** and my low pay leave little surplus.
do: Keep **corrugator shifts** and measure first sheets.
Compare **occasional AI notes** with actual orders.
Save **small fresh-pay amount** only after rent and food.
feel: **Anxious** about routine rent pressure despite little AI change.
S0.quote: A quiet AI year still has a rent date.
fieldNote: His **technical diploma** and strong lead skill do not bring matching pay.
The **three-week reserve** explains baseline anxiety; new saving depends on actual fresh-pay surplus.

Save small amount from fresh full wages only after essentials
Raise lead-operator wage scale at union meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say let the office automate purchase lists, but show our crew the paid hours before a new stacker arrives. I would try a setting chart if another operator has proved it on old board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot stacker might remove the second operator and push a faster pace onto my shift. We cannot afford a cut to my low wage with just three weeks saved and few plants nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union for a written rota and request an offered paid practice slot on rejected board with the stacker isolated and the setter beside me. If that place opens, I would learn the new AI flute-pressure chart and compare alerts with measured sheets; after actual hour cuts, I would apply for posted reachable lead roles only at bill-covering net pay after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about hours and willing to learn a tested chart. A screen can call a sheet straight while the corner still catches your thumb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you run the stacker immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The setter must isolate it and let us practise on rejects during paid time before any live change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What counts as a useful job posting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real lead role with written weekly pay and hours that cover rent after the trip. A noticeboard full of distant work is no cushion.

say: I would demand **written paid hours** before the stacker changes.
I would try a **proved pressure chart** on rejected board.
think: Robot stacking may cut **my paid hours** on the corrugator shift.
Thin **savings and few plants** make a poor offer dangerous for our rent.
do: Request **written corrugator rota** through the union.
Learn **new AI pressure chart** only in offered paid isolated practice.
Apply after **hour cuts** for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay lead work.
feel: **Anxious** about a plausible cut to the household wage.

fieldNote: His **occasional AI use** supports conditional learning of a new production chart.

steps.text: Request written corrugator paid rota through union
Learn new AI flute-pressure chart in offered paid isolated practice
Apply after cuts for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay lead-operator job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2028 finds me sixty, and capable board-handling robots around 2031 find me sixty-three. The planning desk changes first, and then the corrugator crew could be cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the plant to remove our whole night shift when robots can feed and stack board. Nia’s laundry hours and three weeks saved cannot carry the rent, and there are few nearby factories; I lie awake when the rota is late even now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union for dated staffing and severance terms, and cancel the planned family trip. I would apply for posted reachable corrugator or warehouse jobs with bill-covering pay after travel before resigning; if the shift ends without an adequate offer, I would ask the housing office about available support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed about a large wage loss. A good first sheet cannot pay rent if nobody pays the operator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if actual retirement income and Nia’s confirmed wage covered housing, food and health costs. We have no such figures, so I would keep earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would grown children contribute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have homes and bills of their own. I could ask for a lift to an interview, not for their wages.

say: I would ask for **dated staffing terms** before robots arrive.
I would demand **written severance** through the union.
think: I expect **the whole night shift** to end around 2031.
Three **weeks saved** and Nia’s part-time pay cannot carry rent.
do: Request **dated staffing and severance** through the union.
Cancel **planned family trip** to protect rent money.
Apply for **posted reachable jobs** at bill-covering net pay before resigning.
feel: **Alarmed** and sleepless over expected major wage loss.
S2.quote: A good first sheet cannot pay rent if nobody pays the operator.
fieldNote: Expected **whole-shift loss** supports alarm despite his high skill and technical diploma.
The **job path** requires postings, net pay after travel and a real offer before resignation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2031 finds me sixty-three, and capable corrugator robots around 2034 find me sixty-six. Five years could be enough to teach an operator how to maintain the feed rollers properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My two-year diploma and repair experience give me a start, but a maintenance qualification needs supervised work on an isolated line. We cannot spare unpaid weeks, and a course means little unless a reachable posted job pays enough after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid shift and ask the union and plant for a funded paid-time course. If offered an actual place with a fitter supervising safe roller practice and a posted reachable maintenance role at bill-covering net pay, I would enrol; after qualifying I would apply for the role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about our thin cash cushion but willing to learn on a stopped line. A leaflet cannot show where a roller bites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would supervise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A qualified fitter would isolate the drive and watch my first adjustment. I would need an actual paid place, not a promise that seats may appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If no place appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid shifts and search posted operator roles after hour cuts. I would not spend rent money on a private course.

say: I would seek **paid roller-maintenance training** before capable factory robots arrive.
I would require **posted local wages** that cover rent after travel before enrolling.
think: My **diploma and repairs** give a start, not the required qualification.
An **unpaid course** would take money needed for rent.
do: Enrol in **funded maintenance course** only with offered paid safe practice and adequate posted role.
Apply after **qualification** for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay maintenance work.
feel: **Anxious** about thin reserves, open to proven supervised training.
S3.quote: A leaflet cannot show where a roller bites.
fieldNote: His **steady adaptability** supports proven instruction, with no automatic new qualification.
The **later application** requires an offered funded paid safe place and posted reachable adequate job.

Apply after qualification for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay maintenance role
Search posted operator jobs after cuts if no course place opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2036 finds me sixty-eight, and capable board robots around 2039 find me seventy-one. Ten years gives Nia and me time to see whether retirement is an income plan or just a birthday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I had hoped to stop full-time shifts around sixty-seven, but three weeks saved and rent do not support that by themselves. I do not know any pension amount, and Nia’s future laundry hours are not guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep leading the corrugator shift and save a small amount from fresh full wages only after rent and food. I would request retirement and rent figures; if verified household income covers housing, food and health costs at sixty-seven I would leave factory work then, otherwise keep safe paid work, and after 2036 compare posted reachable bill-covering jobs only if still employed and hours fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious even with a longer warning because the rent is due now. I want a last day that does not send my partner to borrow for groceries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If retirement figures fall short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep safe paid work and compare posted wages after travel if shifts fell. I would not stop because a calendar said sixty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own households. We would tell them our decision but not budget their wages.

feel: **Anxious** because low pay and thin savings remain now.

fieldNote: His **planned normal exit** depends on verified income without assumed pension entitlement.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable board robots around 2031 could end the night shift while rent remains due. Written staffing terms, offered funded paid safe maintenance training and a posted reachable job at bill-covering pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask which sheet came off the corrugator first after a flute change. A careful operator can tell you more from that corner than a meeting slide can.

headlineQuote: A careful operator can tell you more from that corner than a meeting slide can.
portrait: **Aaron**, 58, is a senior corrugator lead with a two-year technical diploma and among the best tuning skills at the plant.
His **low lead pay**, part-time laundry partner Nia, grown children, rent, three-week reserve and few nearby plants constrain him.
He uses **AI occasionally** and would learn a new pressure chart only through offered paid isolated practice.
Expected **2031 shift loss** alarms him; a planned age-sixty-seven exit requires verified household income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because 2031 board robots could end the night shift while rent remains due.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing terms**, offered funded paid safe training and posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work would help.
